questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] async report exports for a multi-tenant CRUD app: queue, claim, stream, deliver (organized-experiment-zz7, docs/learning/flow-traces.md). Scenario: VendorOS serves 400 procurement teams; the largest holds 900,000 purchase orders across five years; analysts queue about 3,000 exports a day, with a burst of 300 in the first hour of month-end close; one 'all spend' export is 600,000 rows, roughly 150 MB of CSV that finance opens in Excel; files are kept for 7 days; and an auditor must be able to say, for any file, who asked for it and exactly which filters produced it. Write your design before you look: what the request that queues an export does and returns, what runs the job and how a job is taken by exactly one runner, which version of the saved report a job uses, how 600,000 rows get from Postgres into a file without holding them all in memory, where the file lives and how a user downloads it, who may export what, how the CSV stays correct in Excel, and what the user sees while waiting. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] The queue request only records intent: it loads the saved report inside the caller's tenant, inserts a PENDING export job carrying a copy of the report's dimensions, metrics, filters and name plus the requester, writes a 'queued' audit row, and answers 201 with the job. Generation never happens in that request; a worker does it later. As built the job insert and its audit row are two separate writes, so one can exist without the other; put both in one transaction.

[w3] A job must be taken by exactly one runner. As built the runner selects the oldest ten PENDING rows for the tenant and then flips each to RUNNING with an unconditional update by id, so two runners that overlap both process the same jobs. Claim with a conditional update that only matches a still-PENDING row and check that it changed one row (or select with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in raw SQL), and give the claim a lease so a crashed runner's job can be taken again.

[w3] The job should run from its own copy of the definition, re-parsed through the same zod filter schema that validated the save; as built the runner ignores the copy, reads the live report's filters and only casts them. A Json column does not keep types: the schema coerces the dates to Date objects, but what comes back from the database is text, so a runner that trusts a TypeScript cast is filtering with strings.
keyPoints.quote: JSON has no date type, so the `Date` objects are stored as ISO strings.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Rows are streamed, not collected. As built the report builder loads every matching purchase order with its vendor in one findMany with no take, maps them, and only then filters in JavaScript, so the 600,000-row export sits in the Node heap as Prisma objects and again as mapped rows. Push every filter into the Prisma where clause, read in keyset chunks of a few thousand by id, and pipe each chunk through a CSV encoder into a multipart upload, so memory stays flat whatever the row count.

[w2] Success must mean a file exists. As built a finished job records a generated file name, the row count and a 10-row preview, and that preview overwrites the definition copy, so there is no file, and the job no longer records which filters, dimensions and metrics it was queued with. Write the file to object storage under a tenant-and-job key, keep size and checksum on the job, hand out a short-lived signed URL only after re-checking the downloader's rights, and let a lifecycle rule delete it after 7 days. The storage piece is a supposition: the repo has none.

[w2] An export is a read path, so it needs the read rights of the data it contains. As built the ANALYST role holds the export permission but not the purchase-order read permission, while a spend export lists PO numbers, vendors and amounts; VIEWER is the reverse. Map each report type to the entity permissions it reveals and check them when the job is queued and again when it runs.

[w2] The file has to survive Excel. Amounts leave Prisma's decimal type as JavaScript numbers, and the vendor-performance report adds them up as floats, so a total of 0.10 and 0.20 lands in the export as 0.30000000000000004: sum in SQL or with a decimal type and write amounts as strings. Quote fields that hold commas, quotes or line breaks, and neutralise any user-typed cell that begins with =, +, - or @, because vendor names are user input and a spreadsheet executes them as formulas.

[w1] While it waits, the user sees the job's state: the client polls the job (React Query with a refetch interval that stops at SUCCEEDED or FAILED) or is notified when it finishes. As built nothing in the UI queues an export at all: the Queue export button only logs to the console.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — month-end close, first hour. Two analysts trigger the runner within a second of each other and the auditor finds two 'completed' records for one export, both crediting someone who never asked for it; finance's March-only spend export contains five years of orders; a report edited at 09:05 changes what an export queued at 09:00 contains; a deploy at 09:10 leaves 40 jobs showing RUNNING forever and the dashboard's 'exports running' count never drops; the 900,000-order tenant's export makes the web instance stall for everyone on it; and a failed job shows a raw database error to every report reader. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The double run is the missing claim seen from the audit trail: both runners mark the same rows RUNNING and SUCCEEDED by id with no status condition, so each job completes twice and gets two completion audit rows, and those rows name the runner as actor rather than the person who queued it. The conditional claim fixes the duplicate; record the requester on the job's audit rows and the runner separately.

[w3] The five-year file comes from the date filter silently doing nothing: the row's Date is compared with the stored text, the text converts to NaN, and every comparison with NaN is false, so no row is ever excluded by date. Re-parsing the stored filters with the zod schema turns them back into dates; a test with a saved range and a row outside it would have caught it.

[w2] The changed export is the runner reading the report's current filters through the job's relation instead of the copy taken at queue time, so whoever edits a saved report rewrites every export still waiting on it. Run from the job's own copy; an edit only affects jobs queued after it.

[w2] The 40 stuck jobs have nothing that notices them: RUNNING is set with a start time, no lease, heartbeat or timeout exists, and nothing ever moves a RUNNING job back. The dashboard counts PENDING and RUNNING together and shows them as 'exports running', so the number never drops. A sweeper re-queues jobs whose lease expired, up to a retry limit, then fails them.

[w3] The stall is placement: the runner is an HTTP route any non-VIEWER member can call, so the heaviest work in the system runs inside a web request, on the web tier's event loop and heap, next to everyone else's requests. Move generation to a separate worker pool with a concurrency limit per tenant (one or two jobs at a time) and a row cap per export, so one tenant's close cannot slow another's pages.

[w1] The raw error is stored as the thrown message and returned by the job serializer to anyone who can read reports. Store a stable error code and a user-facing reason on the job, and keep the internal message in logs keyed by the job id.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your export design against the alternatives: generating the file in the request and streaming it straight to the browser versus a queued job; a Postgres job table versus a message broker or a hosted queue; running from a copy of the definition taken at queue time versus the live saved report; keeping the file in object storage versus in a database column versus regenerating it on every download; a runner each tenant triggers for itself versus one shared worker for all tenants; and keeping export history after its report is deleted versus letting it go with the report. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Streaming in the request is the simplest thing that works for small exports (a few thousand rows, a few seconds): no job state, no storage, no polling. It ties up a request and a connection for the whole run, dies at the first proxy timeout with nothing to resume, cannot be retried without redoing the work, and leaves no record. A job costs a state machine, storage and a waiting UI, and buys survivable, auditable, retryable work; many products do both, with a row threshold deciding which path a request takes.

[w3] A job table in the same Postgres lets the job row commit in the same transaction as the request's other writes, is queryable with plain SQL, and needs no new infrastructure; its costs are polling, row churn and hand-built claiming and retries. A broker pushes work and brings retries and backoff, but enqueueing becomes a second write outside the database transaction, so you either accept lost or phantom jobs or add an outbox. The existing composite index on tenant, status and request time is exactly the polling access path.

[w2] A copy at queue time makes an export reproducible and auditable (the file matches what was asked for, whatever happens to the report later) at the cost of a few kilobytes per job and of queued jobs not picking up a fix to the report. Reading the live report picks up fixes but means queued work can change under the requester.

[w2] Object storage with signed URLs keeps large files out of the database, offloads download bandwidth and supports expiry rules, at the cost of a second system whose links must be short-lived and whose keys must be tenant-scoped. Bytes in a database column are transactional and simple but bloat backups and the table; regenerating on download stores nothing but gives a different file each time the data has moved.

[w2] A runner each tenant triggers for itself never queues one tenant's jobs behind another's (though, run inside the web tier, they still share its CPU and memory) and keeps every run inside one tenant's scope, but nothing runs unless someone triggers it. One shared worker runs everything promptly, but needs fair scheduling (round-robin across tenants, a per-tenant concurrency cap) or a tenant that queues 300 exports at close pushes every other tenant's exports behind its own.

[w1] As built the schema cascades a saved report's deletion to its export jobs (no route deletes reports yet), so the job rows, with their requester and filter copy, would go with it; only the audit rows (actor, job id, format) would survive, without the filters. Keeping history (a nullable report link or a soft-deleted report) preserves the audit answer at the cost of rows that point at a report nobody can open; the files themselves still expire on their own schedule.
